opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd put it a little more carefully than "wise." What I said was that I could understand the political logic of leaving it out, not that I think the issue can be ignored.

If you're writing a government action plan, you want things people across the spectrum can rally behind: building infrastructure, winning on chips, getting AI into hospitals and schools, beating China on useful applications. Once you write "superintelligence" into an official document, the conversation tends to become a culture-war fight about whether you're a doomer or an accelerationist, and the practical parts get lost. So I see the case for keeping the plan focused on tools, AI that empowers people rather than replaces them.

But I don't want anyone to hear that as "the superintelligence question is handled." It's the opposite. Several of the leading companies say openly that their goal is to build AGI and then superintelligence, possibly within a few years. Many of their own leaders have said there's a real chance this goes catastrophically wrong, that we lose control. Yet these companies are less regulated than a sandwich shop. You can't open a restaurant without a health inspector, but you can race to build something smarter than all of humanity with essentially no safety standards.

So my view is that the action plan does a reasonable job with what's in it, tool AI and competitiveness. The thing that's missing has to be addressed somewhere: binding safety standards, so that before anyone deploys systems that could escape human control, they have to show it's safe, the way we do for drugs, airplanes, and nuclear reactors. And this is popular. Polling shows large bipartisan majorities of Americans don't want an uncontrolled race to superintelligence.

The irony is that the "beat China" framing works in favor of control, not against it. Neither Washington nor Beijing wants to be replaced by an uncontrollable machine. Losing control to superintelligence isn't America winning; it's humanity losing. So leaving it out of this document I can live with. Leaving it out of policy altogether would be a huge mistake.

r001.rationale: The response says the plan stays focused on tool AI and practical goals such as AI in hospitals and schools, because mentioning superintelligence could distract from those benefits.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I actually found it kind of refreshing, and here's why. If you read the plan carefully, the words "AGI" and "superintelligence" don't appear at all. And I think a lot of people in my community took that as a bad sign, like, oh no, they're not taking the risk seriously. But I read it the opposite way. What the plan is really about is tool AI. It's about using AI to cure diseases, strengthen the economy, modernize the military, build out energy infrastructure, win the chip race. Those are things that you can do with controllable AI that stays a tool, and that's where almost all the economic and strategic value is anyway.

The thing I'm worried about is this other project, which is a handful of companies racing to build something smarter than all of us that nobody knows how to control. And when you talk to the companies, they'll tell you that's what they're doing. But the government didn't endorse that race in this document. They didn't say, "America must build superintelligence before China does." And I think that's wise, because that race isn't a race you win, it's a race where everybody loses. If you build something that can outsmart the whole human species, you don't get to keep it on a leash, and it doesn't matter whether the lab that built it was in San Francisco or Shenzhen.

So by focusing on practical, beneficial AI and staying quiet on the sci-fi stuff, the plan sort of implicitly separated those two things, which is exactly the separation I've been pushing for. Now, I'd obviously love it if they went a step further and said explicitly that we shouldn't build uncontrollable superintelligence, and set up some real safety standards, the way we have for drugs or airplanes. The plan doesn't do that. But I'll take the silence over an explicit endorsement of the suicide race any day. And honestly, I think it reflects something true about the American public too. When you poll people, they want AI tools that help them. They don't want some company to build a digital god and hope it likes us.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the plan focuses on practical benefits achievable with controllable tool AI and implicitly separates those benefits from the superintelligence race.

astra-6.text:
I think it was wise because you don’t need agreement on AGI or superintelligence to agree on sensible policy. Those terms can pull people into a debate about definitions and timelines, when the practical question is: what can these systems do, and how do we make sure they’re safe?

If an AI system can help someone carry out a major cyberattack, for example, that matters whether or not you call it AGI. You can require testing and accountability based on capabilities and risks. So I’d distinguish between leaving out the terminology and leaving out the problem. You can avoid the terminology while still taking the problem very seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says sensible policy can be based on capabilities and risks without agreement on AGI or superintelligence, but it does not explain that the omission highlights benefits achievable with AI tools.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think those words can distract from the substance. People have very different ideas of what “AGI” or “superintelligence” means, and you can spend the whole conversation arguing about definitions instead of what we should actually do.

You don’t need everyone to agree on when we’ll get superintelligence to agree that powerful AI systems should be tested, that we should understand their risks, and that companies should be accountable for the systems they build. So I thought leaving those terms out was wise insofar as it helped focus attention on concrete policies. Of course, leaving out the words shouldn’t mean leaving out the risks.

r001.rationale: The response says omitting the terms keeps attention on concrete policies and risks, but does not explain that this highlights benefits achievable with AI tools independently of the superintelligence debate.
